passages.happening:
Jesus goes back to his hometown, Nazareth, with his disciples. On the Sabbath he teaches in the synagogue. The people are amazed, but not in a good way. Where did he get all this? Isn't he just the carpenter, Mary's son, whose brothers and sisters still live here? “And they took offense at Him.”

Jesus answers that a prophet is honoured everywhere except in his own town, among his relatives, and in his own house. He could do no mighty works there, apart from laying his hands on a few sick people and healing them. And he was amazed at their unbelief.
passages.hearers:
Nazareth was a small farming village in the hills of Galilee. Estimates vary, but most scholars think a few hundred people lived there. In a place that size, everyone knew everyone. They had watched Jesus grow up.

The word for ‘carpenter’ is the Greek tektōn, a builder or craftsman, usually one who worked in wood. Justin Martyr, a Christian writer of the second century, says Jesus made ploughs and yokes. A village builder was a respected working man. He was not a rabbi. To the people of Nazareth, a builder who now taught like a prophet seemed to be getting above himself.

The brothers named here appear again in the New Testament. James later led the church in Jerusalem, and Paul calls him “the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19). The Jewish historian Josephus also mentions him. He says that around AD 62 the high priest had James, ‘the brother of Jesus who was called Christ’, put to death by stoning.

Christians have understood these ‘brothers and sisters’ in three ways: as later children of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view), as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage (the Orthodox view), or as cousins (a long Catholic view). The note on Mark 3 says more.
passages.hard: Mark says Jesus “could not perform any miracles there.” Does that mean his power was limited by their unbelief? Mark does not mean Jesus was weak. In fact he still healed some sick people. In Mark, Jesus' mighty works are not shows put on to force belief. They are acts of rescue for people who come to him in trust. Where people refuse to come, there is little to receive. Matthew tells the same scene by saying he “did not” do many miracles there, because of their unbelief (Matthew 13:58). The point is about the town's closed hearts, not Jesus' strength.
passages.asks: The people of Nazareth thought they already knew everything about Jesus. Familiarity closed them off. Ask whether you have grown so used to Jesus, perhaps from childhood, that you no longer expect him to surprise you. Jesus was amazed at their unbelief. What would amaze him about yours, or about your faith?

passages.happening:
Jesus sends the Twelve out two by two and gives them authority over unclean spirits. They are to take a walking stick and sandals, but no bread, no bag, no money, and no spare tunic. When they are welcomed into a house, they are to stay there until they leave the town. If a place will not welcome them or listen, they are to shake the dust off their feet as they go.

So they go. They call people to repent, drive out many demons, and anoint many sick people with oil and heal them.
passages.hearers:
Travelling with nothing meant depending on others. The disciples could not buy food or a bed. They had to be taken in. In that world, welcoming a guest was a serious duty, and staying in one house showed that they were not shopping around for the best host.

Shaking the dust off your feet was a public sign of breaking off. Paul and Barnabas did the same when a city drove them out: “they shook the dust off their feet in protest against them” (Acts 13:51). It said, in effect, ‘We have done our part. What you do with the message is now yours to answer for.’

Olive oil was a common medicine. The Good Samaritan pours oil and wine on the wounded man (Luke 10:34). Later, James tells the church to pray over the sick and “anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5:14).
passages.asks: Jesus sent them out without the things that make us feel safe. They had to trust God and depend on strangers. Ask what you hold on to so tightly that it keeps you from going where God sends you. And notice that they went two by two. Who has God given you to go with?

passages.t: The death of John the Baptist
passages.happening:
News about Jesus reaches King Herod. Some say Jesus is John the Baptist risen from the dead. Others say he is Elijah, or one of the old prophets. Herod is sure: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!”

Then Mark tells how John died. Herod had married Herodias, his brother's wife. John told him plainly that this was against God's law, and Herod had him chained in prison. Herodias wanted John dead, but Herod held back. He feared John, knew he was a holy man, and liked to listen to him, though it troubled him.

At Herod's birthday feast, Herodias's daughter danced for the guests. Pleased, Herod swore to give her anything, up to half his kingdom. Prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head on a platter. Herod was very sorry, but he would not break his oath in front of his guests. He sent an executioner. John's disciples came and buried his body.
passages.hearers:
This Herod is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. He ruled Galilee from 4 BC to AD 39. Rome never gave him the title of king; Matthew rightly calls him “Herod the tetrarch” (Matthew 14:1), a ruler of part of a kingdom. Mark's ‘King Herod’ may be how ordinary people spoke. Later, Antipas asked the emperor to make him a king. Instead, in AD 39, he was accused of plotting and sent into exile in Gaul, and Herodias went with him.

The marriage was a public scandal. Herodias had been married to Antipas's half-brother, and to marry her Antipas divorced his first wife, the daughter of Aretas IV, king of the Nabateans. The law forbade a man to marry his brother's wife (Leviticus 18:16). Years later, around AD 36, Aretas defeated Antipas in battle.

Josephus also tells of John's death. He calls John a good man, says he was imprisoned and killed at Machaerus, a palace fortress east of the Dead Sea, and gives a political reason: Herod grew suspicious of John's influence over the crowds. Josephus adds that some Jews saw Herod's defeat by Aretas as God's punishment for killing John. Mark tells the personal story and Josephus the political one. A prophet who condemned the ruler's marriage in public was both a personal enemy and a political danger.
passages.ot:
The story is full of echoes. A weak king, a wicked queen who wants the prophet dead, and a prophet dressed like Elijah (1:6): these are Ahab, Jezebel, and Elijah all over again (1 Kings 19:2; 21:25). Later Jesus says of John, “Elijah has indeed come, and they have done to him whatever they wished” (9:13). This time Jezebel wins.

The king's promise, “up to half my kingdom,” echoes the Persian king's words to Queen Esther, “Even up to half the kingdom” (Esther 5:3). And a royal birthday feast that ends in a death recalls Pharaoh's birthday, when one servant was restored and the other hanged (Genesis 40:20-22).
passages.hard: Why does Mark tell this story here, in the middle of the disciples' mission? He sends the Twelve out in verses 7 to 13 and brings them back in verse 30. In between he tells how John was killed. Mark often places one story inside another so that each explains the other. Those who preach repentance, as John did and as the Twelve now do, may meet John's end. And John's death foreshadows Jesus' own: a ruler who knows the man is innocent, a crowd to please, and a body laid in a tomb by his followers.
passages.asks: Herod liked listening to John, but he would not change. In the end he chose his pride and his guests over a holy man's life. Ask where you enjoy hearing the truth but quietly refuse to act on it. And ask what promises or pressures might lead you to do what you know is wrong.

passages.happening:
The apostles come back and tell Jesus all they have done. So many people are coming and going that they cannot even eat. Jesus says, “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while.” They go by boat, but the crowds run ahead along the shore and get there first.

When Jesus sees them, he has compassion, “because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” He teaches them for a long time. Late in the day the disciples want to send everyone away to buy food. Jesus says, “You give them something to eat.” They have only five loaves and two fish. Jesus has the people sit in groups on the green grass. He takes the bread, looks up to heaven, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to the disciples to hand out. Everyone eats and is satisfied. The leftovers fill twelve baskets. About five thousand men have eaten.
passages.hearers:
The disciples' answer shows the size of the problem. A denarius was a day's wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). Two hundred denarii was most of a year's pay, and even that would not have fed the crowd. And Mark counts only the men. Matthew adds, “in addition to women and children” (Matthew 14:21).

A ‘solitary place’ is the same word as ‘wilderness’ at the start of Mark. A Jewish hearer would remember that God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness for forty years (Exodus 16:35). Here is food in the wilderness again.

The twelve baskets of leftovers have made many readers think of the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles. There is more than enough, and some for later.
passages.ot:
‘Sheep without a shepherd’ is from Moses, who prayed that God would give Israel a leader “so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd” (Numbers 27:17). Through Ezekiel God promised, “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them” (Ezekiel 34:23). Jesus first teaches the sheep, then feeds them.

The green grass may recall Psalm 23: “He makes me lie down in green pastures” (Psalm 23:2). The groups of hundreds and fifties recall how Moses organised Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 18:21). And the prophet Elisha once fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, saying, “They will eat and have some left over” (2 Kings 4:43). Jesus feeds thousands with five.

The four actions, took, blessed, broke, and gave, come back at the Last Supper, when Jesus “took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples” (14:22).
passages.asks: Jesus had planned to rest. When the crowd came, he did not see an interruption. He saw sheep without a shepherd. Ask how you see the needy people who interrupt your plans. And notice his words to the disciples: “You give them something to eat.” He asks them to bring what little they have and let him use it. What small thing might you bring?

passages.happening:
Right away Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat while he sends the crowd home. Then he goes up a mountain to pray. By evening the boat is out in the middle of the lake, and the disciples are straining at the oars against the wind.

Very early in the morning Jesus comes to them, walking on the water. Mark says “He intended to pass by them.” When they see him they think he is a ghost and scream. At once he speaks: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.” He climbs into the boat and the wind stops. They are completely astonished, “for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.”
passages.hearers:
The ‘fourth watch of the night’ was the Roman name for the last stretch of the night, from about 3 to 6 in the morning. The disciples had been rowing against the wind for hours, most of the night.

This is Mark's second scene in a boat at night on the lake. In the first (4:35-41), Jesus was asleep in the boat and the disciples woke him. Here he is not with them at all. He is on the mountain praying, yet he sees them struggling and comes to them across the water.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, walking on the sea is something only God does. Job says God “alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8).

The strange words ‘He intended to pass by them’ also have a history. When God showed himself to Moses, he said, “when My glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock” (Exodus 33:22). To Elijah on the mountain, “the LORD is about to pass by” (1 Kings 19:11). The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb as Mark. ‘Passing by’ is how God shows himself.

Jesus' words ‘It is I’ are, in Greek, egō eimi, which can also be read ‘I am’. It is an ordinary way to say ‘It's me’. But it is also how the Greek Old Testament gives God's own words, “I am He” (Isaiah 43:10). Scholars debate how much Mark means by it here. In the setting, with Jesus treading on the sea and passing by, many readers hear more than ‘it's me’.
passages.hard:
Why would Jesus mean to ‘pass by’ his struggling friends? It sounds as if he planned to walk past them. But in the light of the Old Testament, ‘passing by’ is not ignoring. It is God letting himself be seen. Jesus is showing them who he is, as God showed his glory to Moses and Elijah. And the moment they cry out, he turns, speaks, and gets into the boat.

And why were their hearts ‘hardened’? This is the same language used of Jesus' enemies (3:5). Mark does not spare the disciples. They had just seen five thousand fed, and still they did not see who Jesus was. Their problem was not lack of evidence but slowness of heart.
passages.asks: Jesus saw the disciples straining against the wind while he was far away on the mountain. They did not know he saw them. Ask where you feel you are rowing hard, alone, and getting nowhere, and whether you believe he sees. And ask what you have already seen of Jesus that you have not yet let change your heart.

passages.happening: They come ashore at Gennesaret, by the lake. As soon as they step out of the boat, people recognise Jesus. They run all over the area and carry the sick on mats to wherever they hear he is. In villages, towns, and farms, they lay the sick in the market places and beg to touch just the fringe of his cloak. And all who touch him are healed.
passages.hearers:
The word Mark uses for the ‘fringe’ of the cloak is the same word Matthew uses for the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their clothes (Matthew 23:5). The law told Israel to wear them as a reminder of God's commands: “These will serve as tassels for you to look at, so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD” (Numbers 15:39). Jesus wore the clothes of a faithful Jew.

The people remember the woman in chapter 5 who touched his cloak and was healed. Now crowds do the same. The market place, the busiest public space in any town, becomes a place of healing.
passages.asks: The people of Gennesaret did not have deep understanding. They simply knew Jesus could help, and they carried their sick to him. Ask who you could carry to Jesus in prayer today, someone who cannot come on their own. Faith sometimes looks like nothing more than bringing a friend to where Jesus is.
